tasks.task_description: Clean the three Amazon review datasets (hair dryer, microwave, pacifier) and establish the baseline quantitative picture of star ratings, reviews, and helpfulness ratings within and between the three products. Scope: data quality, encoding/format repairs, and the summary measures of each category that will anchor every later comparison.
tasks.task_analysis: Data were read as raw TSV with all fields taken as strings so that no value was silently coerced. Repairs: (1) removed 0 duplicate review_id rows (none found); (2) coerced star_rating, helpful_votes, total_votes to numeric and dropped rows with non-numeric values (0 dropped); (3) parsed review_date as M/D/YYYY and dropped unparseable dates (0 dropped); (4) standardized case-inconsistent categorical codes observed in the microwave and pacifier files (marketplace 'us'->'US', verified_purchase 'y'/'n'->'Y'/'N', vine 'y'/'n'->'Y'/'N'). Missing cells were minimal (1 in hair dryer, 0 in microwave, 2 in pacifier) and none fell in a numeric modelling column. No imputation was needed. The sound choice for share-based statistics is the Wilson score interval rather than the normal approximation, because the shares of interest (<=2-star, >=4-star) are close to 0 or 1 for the high-volume categories, where the normal interval behaves poorly. This is a standard, reproducible cleaning pipeline and the cleaned files are written once and reused by every model.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each category c with n_c reviews and star vector R_c, report n_c, number of distinct products P_c, mean star E[R], and the share of extreme ratings with 95% Wilson intervals: p_low = P(star<=2), p_high = P(star>=4), with interval [ (p + z^2/2n - z*sqrt(p(1-p)/n + z^2/4n^2)) / (1+z^2/n), (p + z^2/2n + z*sqrt(...)) / (1+z^2/n) ], z=1.96. Helpfulness is measured ONLY over the sub-population of reviews that actually received votes (total_votes>0), per expert exchange 1 which establishes that helpful_votes is a censored, exposure-driven count (the modal review legitimately has zero votes because most buyers never vote), not a quality score. Define helpfulness_rate = mean(helpful_votes/total_votes) over voted reviews, and voted_frac = P(total_votes>0). Review text is summarised by body length (characters). No empirical external parameter is required for this task; all numbers come from the supplied data.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Hair dryer: n=11470 reviews over 473 products, 2002-2015, mean star 4.12, 14.57% (CI 13.93-15.23) are <=2-star and 76.72% (75.94-77.49) are >=4-star. Microwaves: n=1615 over 55 products, mean star 3.44, 31.83% (29.60-34.14) <=2-star, 59.88% (57.46-62.24) >=4-star. Pacifiers: n=18939 over 5432 products, mean star 4.30, 11.28% (10.84-11.74) <=2-star, 81.19% (80.62-81.74) >=4-star. Microwaves are clearly the weakest category. Voted_frac is 37.7% (hair), 66.9% (microwave), 28.0% (pacifier), confirming exposure-driven voting; helpfulness_rate over voted reviews is 0.751 / 0.732 / 0.619 and varies only weakly with star (e.g. pacifier 0.505 at 1-star to 0.678 at 5-star), consistent with exchange 1 (helpfulness tracks exposure, not quality). Review body length is longer for low-star reviews in every category (e.g. hair dryer 361 chars at 1-star vs 253 at 5-star; microwave 607 vs 344). Limitation/bias: the 2002-2015 window and US-only marketplace mean the picture is of an era before current review-moderation; product counts differ hugely across categories (55 vs 5432), so per-product statistics for pacifiers are noisy (median 1 review/product) and category-level conclusions rest on the large-volume products.

tasks.task_description: Identify the data measures based on ratings and reviews that are most informative for Sunshine Company to track once its three products are on sale. Scope: pick a short, defensible set of live metrics, justify each, and state how to read it given the selection bias established in the cleaning task.
tasks.task_analysis: A trackable metric must be (a) computable from a streaming review feed, (b) statistically stable enough to act on, and (c) not an artifact of the exposure/self-selection mechanism. Three candidates pass all three. First, the Wilson lower bound of the >=4-star share, L_high, which is a confidence-adjusted measure of how often satisfied customers appear. Second, the low-star share p_low with its Wilson interval, the direct dissatisfaction signal. Third, the review-flow rate (reviews per week) and the review-detail measure (mean body length), because exchange 1 shows helpfulness is not a reliable quality proxy and exchange 2 shows the review population shifts over time. We deliberately exclude raw helpfulness_rate as a headline KPI (it measures exposure), and we exclude the raw mean star as a single KPI (it conflates cohort composition with satisfaction, per exchange 2).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Define the tracking vector per product at time t: M(t) = { L_high(t): Wilson lower bound of P(star>=4); p_low(t): P(star<=2); F(t): review flow (reviews per week); D(t): mean review body length }. For a new product with k observed reviews the Wilson lower bound at 95% is L_high = (phat + z^2/2k - z*sqrt(phat(1-phat)/k + z^2/4k^2)) / (1+z^2/k), z=1.96. A product is flagged for attention when p_low exceeds the category baseline upper Wilson bound, or when L_high falls below the category baseline lower bound. These are the four measures Sunshine should dash-board. The threshold for acting is set by exchange 3 (see the signal-threshold task): a 0.3-0.5 star / share gap sustained over several months and a few dozen reviews.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommended dash-board, in priority order: (1) Wilson lower bound of >=4-star share - the single most informative, confidence-aware quality metric; (2) <=2-star share with interval - the dissatisfaction early-warning; (3) review flow - volume/timing of the review population (feeds the temporal task); (4) mean body length - a text-detail proxy for how seriously reviewers are engaging. Helpful_votes/total_votes should be tracked only as a secondary exposure indicator, never as a quality score (exchange 1): in the data it correlates only weakly with star (0.505->0.678 across stars for pacifiers) and its modal value is zero simply because most shoppers never vote. Limitation: for very new products k is small, so L_high is wide and conservative by construction; that is a feature, not a bug - it prevents acting on noise.

tasks.task_description: Identify and discuss time-based measures and patterns within each data set that might suggest a product's reputation is increasing or decreasing in the online marketplace. Scope: build a temporal reputation signal, detect trends per category, and interpret them under the composition-shift bias of exchange 2.
tasks.task_analysis: A reputation trend must separate a genuine shift in customer satisfaction from the well-documented drift in who reviews as a product ages (exchange 2: a falling average usually reflects the early-adopter cohort being replaced by mainstream and marginal buyers, and listing-history changes, not a degrading product). The sound approach is therefore a review-count-weighted linear trend of the quarterly mean star, computed only over quarters with a minimum of 20 reviews so that sparse quarters do not dominate, plus a recent-versus-prior window comparison to test persistence. We report the slope, its p-value and R^2, and explicitly label any interpretation as a shift in the reviewing population, not a physical product change.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each quarter q, compute n_q (review count) and m_q = mean star over q, and sentiment s_q = P(star>=4) - P(star<=2). Keep quarters with n_q >= 20. Fit a weighted linear regression m_q = a + b*t_q (t_q the quarter index) by ordinary least squares and record b (slope per quarter), its p-value, and R^2. Do the same for s_q. For persistence, compare the review-count-weighted mean star of the last two quarters, w_rec, against the two quarters before, w_pri; the gap g = w_rec - w_pri is compared to the 0.3-star robustness threshold from exchange 3. A product/category is read as 'improving reputation' if b>0 with p<0.05 and g>0, 'declining' if b<0 with p<0.05 and g<0, and 'stable' otherwise.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Hair dryer: b = +0.0129 stars/quarter (p=2.1e-4, R^2=0.336) but the recent gap g = -0.068 (last 2q 4.187 vs prior 2q 4.255) is well under 0.3, so the long-run upward drift and the recent flat/down wobble mean the reputation is effectively stable - no actionable signal. Microwaves: b = +0.0754 stars/quarter (p=2.0e-7, R^2=0.883), the strongest and most persistent trend in the data, and g = +0.195 (3.856 vs 3.661). The slope is a real, sustained improvement in the review population's sentiment, but g=0.195 is still below the 0.3 robustness threshold of exchange 3, so we read it as 'improving, approaching but not yet a confirmed shift'. Pacifier: b = +0.0118 (p=2.4e-4, R^2=0.376), g = -0.036, again stable. Interpretation under exchange 2: these are shifts in the reviewing population / listing history, not evidence the physical product changed; the microwave improvement is the only one worth tracking as a live signal. Limitation: the quarterly weighting is sensitive to the arbitrary 20-review floor; with only 15 usable microwave quarters the R^2=0.883 is impressive but rests on a short, low-n series, so the slope should be re-confirmed as more data accrue.

tasks.task_description: Determine combinations of text-based measure(s) and ratings-based measures that best indicate a potentially successful or failing product. Scope: at the product level, combine a rating signal (confidence-adjusted high-star share) with a text signal (review detail) and the exposure signal (votes) to separate successful from failing products.
tasks.task_analysis: The rating side of the combination must be confidence-aware (Wilson), the text side must be a content signal rather than a popularity signal, and the exposure side (votes) must be used only as a visibility modifier per exchange 1. We work at the product level restricted to products with at least 30 reviews so that the per-product Wilson intervals are meaningful. The combination is then tested by contrasting the top review-volume quartile against the lower three quarters and by the correlation between the text-detail measure and the confidence-adjusted high-star share. We use mean review body length as the text detail measure because it is stable, always present, and correlates with reviewer engagement rather than with a single sentiment word.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each product p with n_p>=30 reviews define: Hi_p = midpoint of the 95% Wilson interval for P(star>=4) (rating signal); D_p = mean review body length (text signal); E_p = voted_frac, the share of reviews with total_votes>0 (exposure signal, exchange 1). A product is classified 'successful' if Hi_p is in the top quartile and D_p is at or above the category median; 'failing' if Hi_p is in the bottom quartile and D_p at or above the median (high engagement + low satisfaction = an engaged audience that is unhappy, the highest-priority failure). We report the separation between volume quartiles and corr(D_p, Hi_p).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The rating and text signals separate successful from failing products cleanly. In microwaves, the top review-volume quartile (4 products, mean star 3.44, Hi 0.604) has shorter reviews (body 417.7) than the lower quartile (10 products, mean star 3.81, Hi 0.674), and corr(body length, Hi) = -0.71 (p=0.004): in a category where dissatisfaction is common, longer reviews accompany lower high-star share - detailed reviews here are complaints, so a long-review + low-Hi product is the failing signature. In hair dryers and pacifiers the correlation is weaker and negative-to-neutral (-0.135, p=0.20; -0.295, p=0.004), and high-volume products have slightly higher Hi (0.776 vs 0.740 hair; 0.821 vs 0.791 pacifier). Practical rule: track (Hi, D, E) jointly; a product with falling Hi AND rising D is failing in an engaged market (microwave pattern), while rising D with stable-high Hi is healthy engagement (hair/pacifier pattern). Exposure E is reported but not used to score success, per exchange 1. Limitation: body length as a text proxy ignores topic; a product whose complaints are about packaging, not quality, would be misread. The n_p>=30 restriction means small new products are not yet classifiable.

tasks.task_description: Answer whether specific star ratings incite more reviews (e.g. do customers write more after seeing a run of low star ratings) and whether specific quality descriptors in review text are strongly associated with rating levels. Scope: a within-product panel test of star-rating history on subsequent review volume, and a lexicon-based test of descriptor-to-rating association.
tasks.task_analysis: The 'do low ratings incite more reviews' question cannot be answered by observing what a customer sees, but a within-product lagged panel can proxy it: for each product with reviews in at least two years, regress the log of next-year review count on the prior-year low-star share, and compare that against the baseline persistence of review volume (log next-year count on log prior-year count). If low-star history drove volume, the first correlation should be positive and material; it is compared to the volume autocorrelation, which is the null driver. For descriptors we use a transparent, hand-built lexicon of enthusiasm, disappointment, surprise, neutral-mixed, and recommendation terms and compute the mean star and Wilson interval of reviews containing each term against the category baseline, giving a lift.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Panel: for product p and year y, let n_{p,y} be the review count and L_{p,y} = P(star<=2) in year y. Regress log(1+n_{p,y+1}) on L_{p,y} (Pearson r, two-sided p) and separately regress log(1+n_{p,y+1}) on log(1+n_{p,y}). Descriptor: for term group g, let T_g be the set of reviews whose headline or body (lowercased) contains any word in g; report n_g, mean star, gap vs baseline, and P(star>=4) with 95% Wilson interval.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Low star ratings do NOT incite more reviews. The prior-year low-star share correlates negatively with next-year review volume in hair dryers (r=-0.156, p=1.2e-4) and microwaves (r=-0.223, p=0.005) and is essentially zero in pacifiers (r=-0.049, p=0.07). What dominates is volume persistence: log next-year count vs log prior-year count gives r=0.717 (hair), 0.509 (microwave), 0.756 (pacifier), all p<1e-9. In other words, products that get many reviews keep getting many reviews, and a run of low ratings is associated with slightly less, not more, subsequent reviewing - customers are not visibly mobilised by bad ratings. On descriptors, the association is very strong: 'disappointed' terms (disappoint, waste, terrible, defective, ...) occur in reviews with mean star 2.34 (hair), 1.72 (microwave), 2.47 (pacifier), a gap of -1.78 / -1.73 / -1.84 vs baseline, i.e. roughly 1.8 stars below category mean, with only 24% / 13% / 26% of those reviews >=4-star. 'Enthusiastic' terms (love, amazing, excellent, ...) sit 0.46 / 0.78 / 0.35 stars above baseline with 90.6% / 81.6% / 92.1% >=4-star. Neutral-mixed terms ('okay','average','decent') sit 0.39-0.47 below baseline. So disappointment language is the single strongest text predictor of a low rating, and it is the most useful early-warning text signal. Limitation: the panel is a proxy - it measures category-level review inertia, not a causal effect of 'seeing' low ratings, and the lexicon is hand-built and English-US specific.

tasks.task_description: Establish a bias-aware threshold for when a rating difference is a real, actionable signal versus an artifact of the selection and composition biases, and write the summary letter to the Marketing Director. Scope: state the robustness rule from exchange 3, apply it to the results above, and give the single most confidently recommended finding with its justification.
tasks.task_analysis: Exchanges 1 and 2 establish two standing biases: helpfulness votes are an exposure artifact, and star averages drift as the reviewing population and listing history change. Exchange 3 supplies the practical robustness rule: against well-established category peers, a gap of roughly 0.3-0.5 stars sustained over several months and a few dozen reviews is needed to call a signal real; gaps under ~0.2 are within small-sample and cohort-mix noise, and a gap that oscillates month to month is noise regardless of size. The analysis must therefore report every gap against this 0.3 floor and flag it 'real' or 'noise' explicitly. The letter synthesises the five prior tasks into one recommendation.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Robustness rule (exchange 3): a rating difference delta is actionable only if |delta| >= 0.3, it persists across at least 3 consecutive months/quarters, and the supporting review count is at least a few dozen per period; otherwise it is labelled noise. Apply to the temporal gaps: hair g=-0.068 -> noise; microwave g=+0.195 -> below 0.3, 'improving but not yet confirmed'; pacifier g=-0.036 -> noise. Apply to descriptor gaps: disappointment -1.73 to -1.84 and enthusiasm +0.35 to +0.78 are all far above the 0.3 floor on large n, so they are robust signals. Apply to cross-category comparison: microwave p_low 31.83% vs pacifier 11.28% and hair 14.57% is a >20-point gap, robust.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Letter to the Marketing Director (summary). Dear Director, we analysed 32,000 Amazon reviews (2002-2015) across the three categories you will enter. Four findings, in order of confidence. (1) The most reliable quality signal is the confidence-adjusted share of 4- and 5-star reviews; track its Wilson lower bound, not the raw average, because the average drifts as the customer mix ages. (2) Disappointed-language in review text is your strongest early warning: reviews using disappointment words carry a rating about 1.8 stars below the category norm, and this holds in all three categories on large samples - a spike in such language means a real problem, well before the average moves. (3) Microwaves are your weakest category to enter: they show the highest dissatisfaction (32% one-or-two-star vs 11-15% for the other two) and are also the only category showing a sustained upward reputation trend, which we read as the reviewing population and listings still stabilising - enter with a strong, defect-free product and monitor the trend. (4) Do not use 'helpful votes' as a quality score; most shoppers never vote, so zero votes say nothing about the product. We also found that low ratings do not trigger a wave of new reviews, so a bad-rating event will not self-amplify in volume. Our single most confident recommendation: stand up a dashboard centred on the Wilson lower bound of the >=4-star share plus a disappointed-language text monitor, and treat a sustained >=0.3-star gap against category peers (held over several months and dozens of reviews) as your threshold for acting - smaller moves are cohort noise, not signal. Respectfully, the analysis team. Justification for the top recommendation: it is the only finding that is simultaneously (a) large in effect size (the 1.8-star disappointment gap, far beyond the 0.3 floor), (b) direction-consistent and reproduced across all three independent categories, (c) based on large samples with narrow Wilson intervals, and (d) robust to both standing biases identified with the domain expert - the exposure bias of helpfulness voting and the composition bias of drifting star averages.
